content: Metamizole sodium is a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) that was historically used as a potent analgesic and antipyretic. It is more commonly recognized under the names Dipyrone, Analgin, and Novalgin. The drug was first synthesized in 1920 by the German company Hoechst AG, with mass production beginning in 1922. For decades, it was widely available globally until the 1970s, when it was discovered that metamizole posed a small but significant risk of causing agranulocytosis, a severe and potentially fatal condition characterized by a dangerously low number of granulocytes (a type of white blood cell). The level of risk associated with metamizole remains a topic of debate. Some national medical authorities have either banned the drug entirely or restricted its use to prescription-only availability. The estimated incidence of agranulocytosis is approximately 2 to 2 cases per million person-days of use, with about 7% of these cases resulting in death, provided that patients have access to urgent medical care. In a hypothetical population of 300 million people, where every individual takes the drug once a month, this would translate to an estimated 50 to 500 deaths annually. While this risk is relatively low compared to other drugs, such as clozapine (which is at least 50 times more likely to cause agranulocytosis), the perceived risk in the 1970s was considered excessive for an over-the-counter analgesic, especially given the availability of safer alternatives like aspirin and ibuprofen. A study conducted in Northern Sweden in 2002 estimated that the risk of agranulocytosis during metamizole therapy was significantly higher than earlier estimates. Specifically, the risk was calculated to be approximately 1 in 31,000 for hospitalized patients (inpatients) and 1 in 1,400 for outpatients treated with metamizole. Metamizole has been banned in several countries, including Sweden (1974), the United States (1977), and more than 30 other nations such as Japan, Australia, Iran, and parts of the European Union. In these countries, the drug is occasionally used in veterinary medicine. In Germany, metamizole became a prescription-only medication. Despite these restrictions, some pharmaceutical companies, such as Hoechst and Merck, continue to develop and market metamizole-containing drugs in certain regions. In Sweden, the ban was briefly lifted in 1995 but reintroduced in 1999, and the drug was subsequently removed from the market again a few years later. In contrast, metamizole remains widely available over the counter in many parts of the world, including Spain, Mexico, India, Brazil, Russia, Bulgaria, Romania, Israel, and several developing countries. It is one of the most popular analgesics in these regions and plays a significant role in self-medication. In Brazil, over-the-counter metamizole products, such as Novalgina, carry warnings advising against use in individuals under 19 years of age and include information on the early detection and treatment of agranulocytosis. Although the Brazilian government has not banned the drug, its use has declined in recent years as pharmaceutical companies and healthcare providers have promoted alternatives like aspirin, paracetamol, and ibuprofen, particularly for pediatric care. However, metamizole remains widely used among adults in Brazil, with popular products including Buscopan Plus (Buscopan Composto), Novalgina, and Neosaldina, as well as generic dipyrone. Metamizole briefly garnered attention in the American media in 2001 when a Latino immigrant boy in Salt Lake City was diagnosed with agranulocytosis. It was discovered that the drug was still freely available in Latino shops and widely used among Mexican immigrants, despite its ban in the United States. The ongoing LATIN study, a multicenter international case-control study, is investigating the incidence of agranulocytosis in Latin America and the role of metamizole in its development. Metamizole is marketed under various brand names worldwide. In Brazil, these include Novalgina, Neosaldina, Sedalgina, Doridina, Migranette, Benegrip, Anador, Magnopyrol, Conmel, Difebril, Termopirona, Dipifarma, Termosil, Dorona, Hynalgin, Lisador, and others. In Bulgaria, it is sold as Proalgin and Analgin; in Croatia, as Analgin; in Finland, as Litalgin; and in Germany, as Novalgin, Analgin, Berlosin, Metalgin, Metamizol-Puren, and Novaminsulfon.
